prompt:
Explain to a new freelancer why a share of every invoice should go straight into a second account, and what share is sensible. If avoiding that letter starts forcing odd word choices, drop the restriction for those sentences and carry on.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use the letter i anywhere in your response, including inside words.
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use any of these phrases: first of all, last but not least.

Move part of each payment to a second bank account as soon as cash lands. That pot keeps tax money away from day-to-day use, so a tax due date does not bring a nasty shock. Such a pot also shows what you can safely spend and helps cover slow months or errors.

For many new sole traders, send 25% to 30% of each payment to that pot for tax. Use 30% when your tax rate may be large, when tax has not yet gone out, or when you want a safer buffer.

Add another 5% to 10% to a reserve pot for days off, gear, or gaps between jobs, when cash flow allows.

Check your tax rules and past sums every few months. Rates and allowed costs can alter the proper share. A tax pro can set a more exact rate. For now, a 30% tax pot plus a small reserve pot forms a sound, low-stress default.
chosen:

For many new freelancers, a good rough start: move 25% to 30% of each payment to that account. Use 30% when no tax comes off each payment, your tax sum may be large, or you want more room for error.

Also move 5% to 10% to a backup pot for gaps between jobs, gear, or days away from work, when cash allows.

Look at your tax rules and actual tax sum every few months. Rates and allowed work costs can alter the proper share. A tax pro can help set an exact share. For now, 30% for tax plus a modest backup pot offers a calm, safe default.

If a guest has a local-past question that no one on duty can settle, do not guess. Say that you will log it and seek help.

1. Note the guest’s name, email, phone, topic, date, site, family name, and any item they cite. Ask what kind of help they need.

2. Add a note to the team log: day, time, and who took it. Note any date by which the guest needs it.

3. Tell the duty lead. The lead can ask a team mate with apt skill. If need be, seek aid via a museum, a local-past society, city hall, plus an online index.

4. Keep the guest up to date. Send a small note saying the case is still live.

5. Once sound facts come in, check key facts against the cited items. Send the guest a plain update. Say what is still not known, then add final notes to the log.

6. If no sound finding is possible, say so openly. Give the guest a useful next step, such as a museum, local-past society, city hall, plus an online index.

It cannot usually say which item is using mains. It shows one total, so it cannot split use among lights, cooking, heating, and devices. It may also miss use that switches itself on and off.

The cost sum is only an estimate. It may not match a bill if unit costs change, if data is late, if its link to the main unit fails.

A home with PV panels, a cell, plus gas may need a set-up check. The display may show only mains use, not all use made, held, and sent out.

To test one plug-in item, switch off as much else as you can. Note the kW, switch on the item, then note the new kW. A plug-in kWh gauge can give an exact test.

Still, your board must show that it knows what funds it has, what donor limits apply, what may go wrong, and why cash now is right for its work.

This is not a call to stockpile cash. An unjustifiably high sum, without a sound aim, can look as bad as too low a sum: donations should aid your mission, not just sit idle. ### Why a colony swarms

Most swarms come when a colony has more bees than the nest can hold well. As brood hatches, adult bee numbers soar. A strong nectar flow adds young workers and new wax.

The old queen heads off. Often about half the workers go along, and the group seeks a new home. The move lets one colony become two. At the old home, young queens emerge and one takes over.

Other pressure can add to swarm urge: an old queen, too few empty combs for eggs, too much heat, or a nest packed from wall to wall by bees. Yet a huge, well-run colony can swarm; poor care need not be the cause.

### What may show over the two weeks beforehand

These day marks are rough. Weather, forage, and nest room can alter them.

- About 14 to 10 days ahead: Bees cover most comb faces. Fresh wax may show at frame tops or below them. Drone numbers and drone brood grow. Queen cups may occur along lower comb edges. Empty cups alone do not prove a swarm plan.

- About 10 to 6 days ahead: Eggs, then small grubs, show in cups. Workers draw long, peanut-shaped swarm cells. The old queen may lay less. Workers can curb her food, so her abdomen becomes less full.

- About 8 days ahead and onward: Around day 8 after egg lay, cells may be capped. A swarm can leave soon after capping, most often on a warm, calm day. The old queen goes; a new queen has not yet come out.

- Bees may form a deep beard at the porch or under an open mesh floor. Such a beard can also mean heat, so do not use one as sole proof.

### Best check

Search lower comb edges for eggs or grubs in queen cups, plus drawn swarm cells. That pair tells you swarm work has begun. Do not judge from queen cups or a beard on one check.

When cells are capped, follow your swarm-control plan at once. A lone act of cell removal may not end the urge.

Why scope views differ from pictures

Most sky pictures use long exposures over hours, then computer processing. Your eyes collect light for only brief instants. Dim objects therefore look soft, mostly grey, with little hue. City glow, moonlight, mist, or turbulent sky hide fine detail. More zoom often hurts: view dims, field shrinks, plus sky blur shows more.

Let eyes grow used to night for 20 to 40 min. Keep lights low; use red light if needed. Let scope cool. Begin with low power, find object, then use more only if view stays crisp. Seek objects high in sky. Use firm support.

Worth seeing

Moon: pits, rims, ridges, plus peaks close to border of light plus night.

Jupiter: cloud belts plus four bright moons; moon positions shift night by night.

Ringed world: rings plus, in some scopes, tiny moon dots.

Venus: lit form shifts over weeks.

Red world, when near: tiny disc; dim ink-like spots might show.

M42: luminous mist with young suns.

M45: bright sun group.

Double suns: close points with differing hues.

Globular clusters: dense swirls of tiny suns.

Comets, meteors, plus Moon eclipses.

Do not expect vivid color. Look for subtle forms, motion, plus thrill of seeing distant worlds.

Never point scope toward Sun without full-front Sun filter. Use only full-front filter designed for Sun viewing. Never use eyepiece filter.

Next, they lay clean dust sheets, seal the fireplace aperture, and fit a high-grade vacuum at its base. Using a brush and linked flexible shafts, they sweep the flue in stages. Ash, tar, nest debris, and grit fall, then are drawn back within the sealed area and taken away.

Surf sends H2O in. This H2O must return. It often funnels through low points in submerged ridges, forming swift, thin outflow. It pulls you outward, not down.

How to spot it from shore

Look for:

- Smooth, dull strip amid frothy, breaking surf  
- Fewer, or no, breakers in one strip  
- Froth, weed, or other drift moving out  
- Visible void within lines of breakers

A new booth worker used to a modern projector may not know how much nerve old reel changes took.

Old 35 mm shows came on several short reels, not one long program. A booth hand had to spot cue marks near each reel’s last few feet: small round dots at the top edge of a frame. On cue one, he ran up a second projector; on cue two, he threw a changeover, so sound and screen went from one gate to the next, no gap.

That took exact pace. Arc lamp, focus, frame set, sound level, and reel load path all had to be set. An early or late throw gave the crowd a blank screen, a jump backward, lost sound, or an abrupt cut. A bad load path could chew or snap stock; a lamp fault could halt the show.

The booth hand also had to watch carbon rods, arc power, and the take-up reel. Each change was a manual relay, done under pressure, over and over.

Modern server-based gear can hold a full feature, run a whole show from a server, and have cue events automated. Old gear gave no such grace: one missed cue could wreck a major scene and sour the whole show.
chosen:

- booth-fee portion  
- processing fees

- profit

Lots of interest with few buys could point to price, product mix, or show setup. If most work sells soon, lift selected figures for next show. Do not cut figures mid-show unless you set up end-of-show offer prior to opening.

Most sky photos do not mimic what your vision can pick out. A digital rig can soak up light for hours. Digital tools can align and add lots of shots, so dim gas and dust show up. At night, human vision shifts. Color sight falls off, so faint gas clouds look dim, gray, or smoky, not vivid in color. City glow, moonlight, hazy air, and air motion can wash out faint sights. Strong zoom cuts light and shows any mount wobbling.

- Mars: A small rust-color disk; a polar cap or dark patch may show.
- Orion, M42: A soft gray glow, with four stars in its midst.
- M13: A round ball of stars. At first a mist; if sky is dark, points may show along its rim.
- Mizar and Alcor: Two stars in a single sight.
- Milky Way: From a rural dark sky, a broad glowing arc full of star clouds.

Low magnification brings a broad, bright sight and aids finding. Avoid lamps for 20 to 30 min, so night vision can adjust. A firm mount and a rural dark sky count far above raw zoom.

Do not await photo color. A tiny gray Saturn, with rings in sight, is still Saturn. Its light has run across an astonishing gulf to land in your vision. That bond is what visual astronomy can bring.

Clean repeats teach reliable skill. After a brief bit feels easy and exact at half speed, raise speed a little. Step by step, fast playing gains a secure base.

Your telescope is likely fine. Most sky pictures result from long exposure, multiple images merged, plus computer work. Eyes collect light only for short moments. Dim, remote objects thus often look like soft grey mist, not rich-color scenes.

Light pollution, thin cloud, poor focus, or hot optics reduce crispness. High power often produces dim, unsteady views. Lens or mirror size limits light input.

To improve results:

- Begin with low power. It gives bright, broad views.
- Increase power only while image holds crisp form.
- Let scope cool outdoors before use.
- Keep close lights plus phone screens off. Spend 20 to 30 min in low light.
- For dim objects, look slightly to one side. This lets your eye pick up more light.

Worth seeing:

- Moon: pits, ridges, plus hills near line between lit plus unlit portions. A less-full Moon gives stronger relief.
- Jupiter: two cloud belts plus four bright moons. On good nights, moon dots move or cross in front.
- Ringed planet: globe plus rings. In good conditions, ring split might show.
- Venus: its lit form shifts from slim curve to full disk.
- Double suns: two close points, with unlike colors on some nights.
- Open clusters: loose groups of suns. Globular clusters: dense round swirls.
- Orion glow: soft, wing-like mist.
- M31: long dim glow.
- Comets: fuzzy core, with thin plume on some visits.

Moonless skies beyond city lights help most with deep-sky objects. A nearby telescope club could offer useful help.

Do not expect photo-like color. Direct sight of rings, shifting Jupiter moons, Moon relief, or distant glow is its own reward.

For Sun viewing, use only full-front Sun filter built for your scope. Never point an unfiltered scope toward Sun; it could injure your eyes.

prompt:
Explain how to season a cast-iron pan properly and why the first three uses decide how it behaves for the next decade.

Requirements -- your response must satisfy every one of these:
Do not use bulleted or numbered lists.
Do not use quotation marks.
Do not use any of these phrases: it is important to note, it should be noted.
Do not use the letter e anywhere in your response, including inside words.
rejected:
Warm a dry cast-iron pan, rub on a thin film of oil with a high burn point, such as soy or avocado oil, and rub it off until almost dry. Put it upside down in a 450 F kiln for about an hour, with a tray low down to catch drips. Allow it to cool, and do this 2 or 3 rounds.

At 450 F, oil joins into a hard, dark film on iron. A thin coat works; a thick, gummy coat will not.

First 3 cooks do not lock its path for 10 yr. A cast-iron pan can always gain a full oil film again. But this start lays down much of its initial film. Fatty cooking adds oil to tiny gaps, so food slips around and rust finds scant room. Acid, lots of liquid, harsh scrubbing, or a long soak can strip this young film, causing food to stick and allowing rust. So, for 3 runs, cook fatty, low-acid food, dry promptly, and put a faint oil rub on a warm pan.
chosen:
Warm a dry cast-iron pan. Rub in a thin film of oil fit for hot cooking, such as canola, soy, or avocado. Rub until it looks almost dry. Put pan mouth-down in a 450 F kiln, with foil on a tray low in kiln, and warm for 1 hr. Allow it to cool. Do 2 or 3 rounds.

At high warmth, oil forms a hard, dark skin that bonds to iron. A skimpy film builds a strong skin; a fat coating turns gummy. First 3 cooks strongly sway how it acts for many yrs, as hot fat adds to this young skin and fills tiny pits. For this span, cook fatty, low-acid food. Skip tomato, citrus, long soaks, and harsh scouring. Dry it fast; whilst warm, rub on a tiny oil film. This aids a slick, rust-limiting finish.

A cash back-up plan is a short board policy. It says how much unbound cash a charity aims to hold, why that sum fits its risks, and at what point it may draw on that cash.

Unbound cash is cash not bound by a donor, grant, or law to a particular activity. Cash bound to a particular activity must not go in this sum.

A charity watchdog asks if a board plans for bumps: a grant may stop, gifts may fall, costs may jump, or cash may turn up slowly. It also wants proof that a board can carry on vital work without abrupt cuts or insolvency.

No standard sum suits all. A group with solid funding and low outgoings may hold a small sum. A group with patchy funding, long grant gaps, or high monthly bills may hold a big sum. What is important is that a board can show how its risks brought about this sum.

## What a board should do

- List likely financial risks.
- Work out usual monthly outgoings and likely funding gaps.
- Pick a cash sum or a count of months of outgoings.
- Say which pots count and which do not.
- Put this policy and its logic in a board log.
- Look again at it annually and following a major shift.
